Hand-checked: ¹H, ²H, ³H all have Z = 1 with A = 1, 2, 3, so they are isotopes; ¹⁴C (Z = 6) and ¹⁴N (Z = 7) both have A = 14, so they are isobars.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Isotopes
steps.mark_note: Same Z, different A, with example
lines: Isotopes: nuclei with the same atomic
number Z but different mass numbers A are

lines.text: Ex: ¹H, ²H, ³H are isotopes of hydrogen.

steps.margin_note: First mark. The definition needs both halves: same Z AND different A, plus one named example.
steps.why: Z fixes which element it is, so isotopes are the same element with different numbers of neutrons. That is why all three hydrogens sit in one box of the periodic table.
common_mistakes: Writing 'same atomic mass' — isotopes have DIFFERENT mass numbers; it is the atomic number that is the same.
Giving the definition without an example. The example carries part of the credit.

recall.must_convey: That isotopes have the same atomic number Z but different mass numbers A, with an example such as the three hydrogens.
accept: same atomic number but different mass number

steps.memory_tip: isotoPe — the P says same Protons (same Z). isobAr — the A says same mass number A.

steps.label: Isobars
steps.mark_note: Same A, different Z, with example
lines: Isobars: nuclei with the same mass number
A but different atomic numbers Z are

lines.text: Ex: ¹⁴C (Z = 6) and ¹⁴N (Z = 7), both A = 14.
Isotopes: same Z · Isobars: same A

steps.margin_note: Second mark. ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N are different elements with one shared mass number.
steps.why: A counts all the nucleons. Two different elements can still add up to the same A, and that shared total is all that isobars have in common.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two definitions. Isotopes share Z; isobars share A.
Using two isotopes of one element as the isobar example — isobars must be different elements.

recall.must_convey: That isobars have the same mass number A but different atomic numbers Z, with an example such as carbon-14 and nitrogen-14.
accept: same mass number but different atomic number

steps.memory_tip: Keep one pair ready: ¹H, ²H, ³H for isotopes; ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N for isobars.

insider_note: The examiner looks for both definitions and one named example of each; the pair ¹H, ²H, ³H and ¹⁴C with ¹⁴N is enough.
